title: Fine-grained billing sim and autoscale rules (working draft)
body:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures a hands-on simulation and a proposed set of autoscale rules for customer billing alignment during Dedicated capacity POCs. Goal: give SEs a lightweight playbook to estimate customer economics for mixed reserved + burst pools and to produce a small, reproducible simulation they can run during workshops.

Context / why different from other sizing docs:
- Most prior notes focus on pure sizing or pure SLA-driven pool shapes. This is practical for sales demos: reconcile fine-grained per-route billing ideas (metering at slot/throughput level) with the realities of GPU commitment amortization and burst capacity.
- Assumes heterogeneous GPU pool (A100-40GB, L40s, and some spare T4s for embedding-heavy routes).

Quick outcomes (TL;DR):
- Sample 30-day sim (mixed traffic) showed a 22% lower unit cost when booking a 60% reserved commitment vs purely on-demand, assuming we can keep warm prewarmed instances for 40% of peak minutes.
- When prewarm is impossible and tail traffic dominates (spiky <=5min bursts making up 28% of traffic), burst-only strategy beats reserved by ~7% for first 90 days because of lower commitment overhead.

Assumptions used in sims (adjustable params):
- GPU costs: A100-40: $3.60/hr (on-demand list), L40s: $2.85/hr, T4: $0.45/hr. Reserved discount: 40% effective over monthly commit.
- Model footprint: small text gen route -> fits 1 A100 (peak batch small), chat-heavy route -> needs L40s for latency targets when concurrent sessions >100.
- Prewarm cost: holding a GPU idle counts 100% of hour. We model prewarm as continuous reservation vs ephemeral spin-up with 45s cold start and 20s additional tail latency.
- Traffic shape: 7-day weekday pattern + random spikes (Pareto 80/20 for session contribution).

Simulation design (how to run):
1) Input: minute-level QPS distribution for target routes (csv).
2) Policy knobs: reserved_commit_percent (0-100), burst_limit_gpus, prewarm_targets_by_route (min GPUs), scale_up_cooldown, scale_down_cooldown.
3) Cost model: per-minute amortized reserved cost + per-minute on-demand cost for burst capacity + token-based variable cost (simulated at 0.0008 $/1k tokens baseline).
4) Outputs: monthly cost, average tail latency, percent of requests served by reserved vs burst, wasted prewarm minutes.

Representative policy examples (to try during POC workshops):
- Conservative: reserved_commit=70%, prewarm_targets_by_route: {chat:2, generation:1}, burst_limit=20% of pool, scale_up_cooldown=30s, scale_down_cooldown=8m. Use when customer expects steady enterprise traffic and SLAs matter.
- Cost-first: reserved_commit=40%, prewarm_targets_by_route: {chat:1}, burst_limit=50% of pool, aggressive scale_down_cooldown=3m. Use for startups or unpredictable demos.
- Hybrid with bucketed metering: reserved_commit=50%, and for each route we maintain a bucket of minutes (e.g., route A gets 1000 reserved-minutes/day). Buckets are consumed first; burst consumption is charged as on-demand. This maps neatly to per-route billing proposals (helps finance teams reconcile reservations).

Observed tradeoffs and heuristics from sims:
- Prewarm efficiency: If prewarm minutes are utilized >35% of the time they pay back. Large, steady chat workloads typically pass this threshold.
- Burst window sizing: short burst windows (<=5min) with high frequency favor larger burst budgets but smaller reserved commits. If bursts are long (20m+), reserved capacity becomes more favorable.
- Mixed GPU types: placing low-latency chat onto L40 and batch gen onto A100 gives better amortization; avoid colocating high-memory and embedding-heavy routes on the same reserved pool unless utilization is >60%.

Practical autoscale rules (operator-ready pseudocode for SEs to show customers):
- Rule A (SLA-first):
  - if admitted_latency_95 > target and reserved_available_gpus > 0 then scale_up(reserved) immediately
  - else if admitted_latency_95 > target and reserved_exhausted and burst_available then allocate(burst) up to burst_limit
  - scale_down only after scale_down_cooldown and utilization < 25% for 6m
- Rule B (Cost-conservative):
  - scale_up reserved in 2-GPU increments when sustained utilization > 70% for 3m
  - if spike > 200% of baseline and reserved_exhausted, only allow burst if predicted spike_duration > 10m (avoid paying on-demand for microbursts)
  - proactive prewarm: if schedule.predict(peak_window) then prewarm route-specific GPUs 15m before window

Billing reconciliation sketch (workshop-friendly):
- Map reserved_commit to a virtual SKU called "reserved-GPU-minute". Each route gets an allocation. After month-end reconciliation, unused reserved-GPU-minutes roll into team-level credit or are amortized into next month's bill at 20% discount.
- Metering: shard per-request attribution by token-usage and GPU-minute consumed. Example: a request that used 0.6 GPU-minute from reserved pool consumes 0.6 reserved-GPU-minute and 0 on-demand.
- Show customers a simple CSV output from the sim: columns = minute, route, reserved_gm_used, burst_gm_used, token_count, latency_p95, cost_reserved, cost_burst, billable_total. This gives finance teams an auditable ledger.

Example sim snapshot (30-day condensed):
- Input: average 1200 requests/min weekdays, 420 off-peak; token avg 480 tokens/request; peak 5x baseline for short windows.
- Policy: reserved_commit=60%, burst_limit=30%, prewarm_targets_by_route: chat=2, gen=1.
- Result: monthly_cost = $38,700; reserved_cost_share = $25,000; on-demand_burst = $9,900; token_variable = $3,800. Unit cost per 1M tokens = $30.7.
- Sensitivity: if reserved_commit lowered to 40%, monthly_cost -> $41,600 (worse because burst on-demand premiums). If prewarm infeasible, cost -> $47,200 (cold start overhead and more on-demand usage).

Workshop checklist (what SE should run with customer):
1) Get minute-level QPS export for 7 days (or sample) and token histogram by route.
2) Pick two candidate policies (SLA-first vs cost-first) and run sim for both.
3) Share CSV ledger and a 3-slide summary: cost delta, % requests handled by reserved, recommended commit %.
4) If customer agrees to commit trial: run 14-day shadow run with real routing policy but without committing payments; capture utilization and missed SLOs.

Open questions / follow-ups for eng: 
- Should we add an API-level tracing tag to attribute GPU-minutes to route_id at runtime? (helps reconcile metering).
- How to reflect priority preemption costs when we use spot-like burst instances in Dedicated? Need engineering input on preemption rates in cloud partners.
- Feasibility of exporting the sim ledger in a format that plugs directly to customer billing (CSV -> Quickbooks mapping).

Notes-to-self:
- Prepare an accompanying lightweight Jupyter sim we can use in live demos (param inputs editable).
- Sanity-check the GPU hourly costs with partnerships team before sending to customers.
- Add an appendix with step-by-step commands to set up a 2-node reserved pool and a 1-node burst pool in the POC account.

Appendix (sample CSV ledger header):
minute,route,reserved_gm_used,burst_gm_used,tokens,latency_p95,cost_reserved,cost_burst,cost_tokens,total_cost

End of working draft.

Notes: this is intentionally pragmatic and workshop-focused rather than a canonical sizing doc. Use during customer calls where finance and infra owners are present.
